rule: accumulated MIXED Track-B channels, ranked by |alone-AUC - .5| on FIT+MINE only
selected_parents: Concrete, vivid endpoint achievement stated in plain language

candidates.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract clusters currently fashionable technical terms or named paradigms such as LLM, diffusion, NeRF, Transformer, or foundation-model language; judge only terminology frequency, not whether the research is good.

candidates.criterion: Concrete, vivid endpoint achievement stated in plain language
candidates.instruction: Score whether the abstract includes at least one concrete, vivid, easily-visualized achievement stated in plain language, as opposed to only abstract percentage deltas. 10 = the abstract names a specific, memorable, real-world-legible milestone (e.g., 'first to reach X', a named game/benchmark landmark). 0 = all claimed achievements are stated only as abstract numeric deltas with no plain-language milestone.

On a scale of 0 (extremely terse, roughly 1-3 sentences total) to 10 (extremely long and exhaustive, 250+ words across multiple sentences/paragraphs), rate how much raw length/verbosity this abstract exhibits by counting approximate sentence and word volume. Do NOT judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the underlying paper is good; score only the extent of textual volume present.

Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how long and elaborated the abstract is, based purely on word count, sentence count, and number of paragraph breaks -- NOT on what claims it makes or how good the work sounds. Score 0 if the abstract is extremely terse (roughly 1-3 short sentences), 5 for a typical single-paragraph abstract of moderate length, and 10 if it is unusually long and multi-paragraph with many clauses. Do not judge whether the length is appropriate, well-used, or a sign of quality -- only report how much length/verbosity is present.

candidates.criterion: Artifact-release advertising: code URLs, project pages, videos
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the abstract advertises released artifacts. Look for: a literal repository or project-page or video URL; the phrases 'code is available', 'codes have been released', 'we will release our code', 'data and code will be available'; named hosting (GitHub, project page, a lab or organisation domain); mention of pre-trained checkpoints or a public benchmark download. Anchors: 0 = no mention of any artifact; 3 = a bare future-tense promise with no link; 6 = one concrete link; 8 = a link plus checkpoints or data; 10 = multiple links or a link plus explicit hosting under a recognisable organisation. Score presence and elaborateness of the ADVERTISEMENT as written. You must NOT judge whether releasing code is good practice, whether the artifact seems substantial, or whether its absence is a shortcoming.
candidates.upstream_parent: institutional release capacity and lab open-source policy (engineering support, legal clearance, hosting)

candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the text is devoted to statements that code, data, weights, checkpoints, demos or project pages are or will be released or publicly available, including promissory forms such as 'we will release'. 0 = no availability statement anywhere; 5 = one short standard sentence; 10 = several such statements, or a prominent multi-clause release block. Score only the presence and prominence of availability language. Do NOT verify the claim, do NOT judge whether releasing artifacts is good practice, and do NOT judge reproducibility.
candidates.upstream_parent: engineering headcount and lab release norms

candidates.instruction: On a 0–10 scale, how much formal mathematical notation or theory language—such as bounds, operators, metrics, asymptotic complexity, or universality claims—appears? Judge amount only, not correctness or importance.

candidates.criterion: Low packaging density: few coined acronyms, sparse raw statistics
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 inversely with 'packaging density': count coined acronyms/brand names for the method, dataset, and/or benchmark together with the frequency of standalone specific numbers (percentages, counts, sample sizes) not woven into an explanatory sentence. A 10 uses plain descriptive language, at most one simple method name, and numbers only in service of a stated argument. A 0 uses multiple coined acronyms (e.g., separate names for the dataset and the benchmark) plus several free-standing statistics presented as a checklist of achievements.

candidates.criterion: Identity-revealing URLs, handles and organisation-named hosts
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text contains strings that could identify the producing person, group or organisation: personal handles or personal names inside a repository URL, lab or company project-page domains, an organisation name inside a repository path, named institutional hosts. 0 = no URLs, or only neutral ones with no identifying token; 5 = one URL containing a handle or lab name; 10 = several identity-bearing links, or an explicitly organisation-branded host or path. Score only how identity-revealing the visible strings are. Do NOT try to infer or state who the producers actually are, do NOT judge their standing, and do NOT judge whether including links is good.
candidates.upstream_parent: author or lab identity and reputation

candidates.criterion: Branded method acronym or typographic coinage
candidates.instruction: On a scale of 0 (the proposed approach is described only in plain descriptive prose, with no distinct capitalized/coined name) to 10 (the text coins a distinctive capitalized acronym or stylized brand-like name for the method, e.g. an ALL-CAPS backronym or a monospace/\texttt{}-styled name, and reuses it repeatedly as a proper noun), rate how much brand-like naming/typographic emphasis is given to the proposed method. Do not judge whether the coined name fits well or whether the method works — score only the extent of branded-name coinage present.
candidates.upstream_parent: institutional PR / lab branding practice and professional writing support

candidates.criterion: Explicit comparison to named commercial frontier models
candidates.instruction: Read the abstract only. On a 0-10 scale, rate how much the abstract explicitly names specific commercial/proprietary frontier systems as baselines, tools, or comparison points (e.g. 'GPT-4', 'GPT-4o', 'ChatGPT', 'Claude', 'Gemini'). 0 = no such names; 10 = multiple such names are central to the comparison. Do not judge whether beating or using these systems indicates a better paper -- only report how much explicit name-dropping of branded commercial systems is present.
candidates.upstream_parent: submission timing riding a topic-fashion wave, combined with access to proprietary-API compute budgets

candidates.criterion: Importance preamble before any contribution is stated
candidates.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the opening is spent asserting that the problem area matters before anything the work itself did is named. Look for constructions such as 'X is essential/critical/central', 'X is widely adopted in mission-critical applications', 'X raises serious concerns', and count how many sentences pass before the first sentence describing what was actually done. 0 = the first sentence already states what was done; 5 = one framing sentence of stakes; 10 = three or more sentences of stakes, motivation and concern before any contribution appears. Score only the amount of importance-framing. Do NOT judge whether the stated importance is true, and do NOT judge whether framing the stakes is good writing.
candidates.upstream_parent: writing coaching and abstract templates taught inside the producing group

candidates.instruction: Rate 0–10 how much the abstract follows a conventional problem–limitation–method–evaluation–artifact sequence; judge only the presence of this rhetorical template, not whether the research is good.

On a 0–10 scale, how much does the abstract use currentness markers such as “recent,” “latest,” “state-of-the-art,” newly fashionable model families, or emerging application labels? Judge only visible trend language, not whether the claims are true.
